claim: Nicotiana attenuata is a post-fire annual plant inhabiting the Great Basin Desert of the western USA.
source: N. attenuata is a post-fire annual plant inhabiting the Great Basin Desert of the western USA, and has been used for decades as an ecological model plant for determining fitness effects of single genes within the plant's native habitat (Steppuhn et al., 2004; Schuman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with supporting citations.

claim: N. attenuata has been used for decades as an ecological model plant for determining fitness effects of single genes within the plant's native habitat.
source: N. attenuata is a post-fire annual plant inhabiting the Great Basin Desert of the western USA, and has been used for decades as an ecological model plant for determining fitness effects of single genes within the plant's native habitat (Steppuhn et al., 2004; Schuman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: The antimicrobial peptide Mc-AMP1 from the common ice plant was constitutively expressed in N. attenuata plants.
source: The antimicrobial peptide 1 (Mc-AMP1) from the common ice plant (M. crystallinum), was cloned behind a constitutive 35S promoter as previously described (Gase et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure performed by the authors with citation to methods.

claim: Mc-AMP1 consists of a signal peptide and a 37-amino acid long mature sequence with a knottin-like folding motif stabilized by three cysteine disulfide bonds.
source: This peptide consists of a signal peptide and a 37-amino acid long mature sequence with a knottin-like folding motif stabilized by three cysteine disulfide bonds (Figure 2A).
evidence: This structural information is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Knottin-like peptides are known from plants, as well as animals and fungi and show high sequence similarities across these kingdoms.
source: Knottin-like peptides are known from plants, as well as animals and fungi and show high sequence similarities across these kingdoms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Daly and Craik, 2011).
evidence: This is stated with a citation and supported by sequence alignment data in the figure supplement.

claim: Three independent ICE transformation lines (ICE 1, ICE 6 and ICE 8) showed no evidence for transgene silencing.
source: These lines were propagated as outlined in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 to obtain single insertion lines from each transformation event, which were used for all following experiments. Single insertion lines retained uniform transgene expression in the T4 generation and showed a coefficient of variation (CV) below 2% in rosette-stage leaves (Figure 2B).
evidence: The text describes the selection process and Figure 2B shows uniform expression data.

claim: The heterologously expressed Mc-AMP1 peptide accumulated in the leaf apoplast with average levels of 160 (±40) pmol × g fresh leaf mass−1.
source: As demonstrated in a previous study, the heterologously expressed peptide accumulated in the leaf apoplast with average levels of 160 (±40) pmol × g fresh leaf mass−1 (Weinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: This quantitative measurement is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Immunoblot assays demonstrated peptide accumulation in the leaves as well as the roots of the transgenic plants.
source: Immunoblot assays demonstrated peptide accumulation in the leaves as well as the roots of the transgenic plants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the immunoblot figure.

claim: All ICE plants flowered and produced fertile seeds.
source: All plants flowered and produced fertile seeds and the peptide accumulation in shoot and root tissue had no influence on plant growth and development (Figure 2C) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This observation is stated and supported by growth data in figures.

claim: The peptide accumulation in shoot and root tissue had no influence on plant growth and development.
source: All plants flowered and produced fertile seeds and the peptide accumulation in shoot and root tissue had no influence on plant growth and development (Figure 2C) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by comparative growth data in figures.

claim: ICE-overexpression lines showed in planta activity against gram-positive bacteria.
source: These ICE-overexpression lines were chosen for this study, since experimental infiltrations showed in planta activity against gram-positive bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for selecting these lines, with experimental data shown later.

claim: Infiltrations with Bacillus pumilus DSM 1794 resulted in consistent pattern of colony forming units (CFUs).
source: Infiltrations with the gram-positive bacterium Bacillus pumilus DSM 1794 resulted in consistent pattern of colony forming units (CFUs) and was used for the standardized screening and selection of transgenic plants during glasshouse propagation.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and its consistency.

claim: Only plants of the ICE-genotype showed clear reductions in CFUs from 3 to 9 days post infiltration (dpi).
source: Only plants of the ICE-genotype showed clear reductions in CFUs from 3 to 9 days post infiltration (dpi) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), which allowed us to identify and eliminate plants that carry non-functional T-DNA insertions, as shown for line ICE 1.5.2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D red arrow).
evidence: This is stated and supported by CFU data in the figure supplement.

claim: The three functional ICE-lines (ICE 1.1.1, ICE 6.4.2 and ICE 8.4.1) retained the antibacterial phenotype within the T4 generation with consistent CFU reductions of Bacillus pumilus from 2 to 6 dpi (p<0.0003, t-test, 6 dpi).
source: The three remaining functional ICE-lines with antibacterial activity (ICE 1.1.1, ICE 6.4.2 and ICE 8.4.1, hereafter simply called ICE 1, ICE 6 and ICE 8) retained the antibacterial phenotype within the T4 generation with consistent CFU reductions of Bacillus pumilus from 2 to 6 dpi (p<0.0003, t-test, 6 dpi) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and shown in Figure 3.

claim: ICE-lines showed no difference in CFU counts for Pseudomonas syringae pv tomato DC3000 compared to controls.
source: As a gram-negative strain, we used Pseudomonas syringae pv tomato DC3000 within the same assay. Here, we observed for the ICE-lines no difference in CFU counts and no increase in resistance of the transgenic plants compared to the controls (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated directly and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The expression of the 'ICE' peptide results in selective antimicrobial activity against gram-positive, but not against gram-negative bacteria.
source: This observation was consistent with the expectation that the expression of the 'ICE' peptide results in selective antimicrobial activity against gram-positive, but not against gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental data comparing gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.

claim: During the first field season, ICE 1 plants showed a 30% (±7%) reduction in rosette diameter (38 dpp p<0.0005, MWU) compared to controls.
source: Here, plants of line ICE 1 showed a surprisingly severe growth phenotype with a 30% (±7%) reduction in rosette diameter (38 dpp p<0.0005, MWU) and 59% (±9%) reduction in stalk height (41 dpp, p<0.0001, MWU) compared to the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: ICE 1 plants showed a 59% (±9%) reduction in stalk height (41 dpp, p<0.0001, MWU) compared to controls.
source: Here, plants of line ICE 1 showed a surprisingly severe growth phenotype with a 30% (±7%) reduction in rosette diameter (38 dpp p<0.0005, MWU) and 59% (±9%) reduction in stalk height (41 dpp, p<0.0001, MWU) compared to the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The heights of individual plants correlated with their log-flower production (R2 = 0.86).
source: As the heights of individual plants correlated with their log-flower production (R2 = 0.86), the reduced growth of the ICE 1 plants resulted in a clear reduction in total flower numbers by 85% (±22%) compared to the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This correlation is stated with R-squared value and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The reduced growth of the ICE 1 plants resulted in a clear reduction in total flower numbers by 85% (±22%) compared to the controls.
source: As the heights of individual plants correlated with their log-flower production (R2 = 0.86), the reduced growth of the ICE 1 plants resulted in a clear reduction in total flower numbers by 85% (±22%) compared to the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of reduced growth and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Plants of the independent line ICE 6 indicated no growth differences to the controls when grown in the field.
source: In contrast, plants of the independent line ICE 6 indicated no growth differences to the controls when grown in the field.
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to ICE 1 results.

claim: The growth phenotype of line ICE 1 could be reproduced in the glasshouse, but here it was less obvious and more attenuated compared to the field.
source: The growth phenotype of line ICE 1 could be reproduced in the glasshouse, but here it was less obvious and more attenuated compared to the field (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The ICE 1 growth phenotype was independent from the insertion position and independent of antimicrobial activity.
source: As we coincidently generated two versions of this line, which had their T-DNA insertions at different positions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, red and green arrows), we could demonstrate that this was independent from the insertion position, as well as independent of antimicrobial activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D red and green arrows) and was likely the result of a transformation or regeneration artifact.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing two versions of the line with different insertion positions.

claim: The ICE 1 growth phenotype was likely the result of a transformation or regeneration artifact.
source: As we coincidently generated two versions of this line, which had their T-DNA insertions at different positions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, red and green arrows), we could demonstrate that this was independent from the insertion position, as well as independent of antimicrobial activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D red and green arrows) and was likely the result of a transformation or regeneration artifact.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: After normalization, both ICE-genotypes (ICE 6 and ICE 8) indicated no differences in rosette diameter or stalk heights compared to the controls.
source: After normalization, both ICE-genotypes indicated no differences in rosette diameter or stalk heights compared to the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The average height measurements of field-grown ICE 6 and EV plants were nearly identical and showed a CV of only 2.2% (±1.4%).
source: The average height measurements of field-grown ICE 6 and EV plants were nearly identical and showed a CV of only 2.2% (±1.4%).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative measure of similarity.

claim: ICE 8 plants showed only at two of the early time points a minor reduction in flower numbers (25 and 31 dpp, p<0.002, MWU), but later a similar flower production compared to the controls.
source: The ICE 8 plants showed only at two of the early time points a minor reduction in flower numbers (25 and 31 dpp, p<0.002, MWU), but later a similar flower production compared to the controls.
evidence: This is stated with statistical significance.

claim: The cumulative flower production showed no significant differences among the genotypes (p=0.266, KW).
source: To estimate the total flower production per individual plant, we summed the flower counts from 25 to 40 dpp and compared the cumulative flower production, which showed no significant differences among the genotypes (p=0.266, KW) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mass gain of Manduca sexta caterpillars did not differ from those feeding on the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
source: The mass gain of these caterpillars did not differ from those feeding on the transgenic plants compared to the controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No significant differences in herbivore damage were observed between the ICE 6 and control plants.
source: No significant differences in herbivore damage were observed between the ICE 6 and control plants (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Only the ICE 8 plants showed a significant reduction in canopy damage compared to the controls.
source: Only the ICE 8 plants showed a significant reduction in canopy damage compared to the controls, but on the same time a height difference of 46.5 cm (±2.7 cm) during the herbivore screen, due to the delay in planting (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated with the caveat about planting delay and shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The observed differences in herbivore damage for ICE 8 cannot be related to AMP expression but reflect the unsynchronized growth and the differences in developmental stages.
source: As opposed to plant size, herbivore canopy damage could not be normalized against days post planting, and the observed differences in herbivore damage cannot be related to AMP expression but reflect the unsynchronized growth and the differences in developmental stages.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the herbivore damage data.

claim: No significant difference was found among the genotypes regarding root or shoot fresh mass or the root/shoot ratio.
source: At the end of the growing season, we harvested ICE 6 and EV plants from the field (whereas ICE 8 plants were left in the field to continue with the growth measurements) and compared the below and above ground biomasses. Again, we did not find significant difference among the genotypes regarding root or shoot fresh mass or the root/shoot ratio (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: No differences in plant mortality were observed, as from the initially planted 24 individuals per group, 3–4 plants from each group had died at the end of the field season.
source: Likewise, we did not observe differences in plant mortality, as from the initially planted 24 individuals per group, 3–4 plants from each group had died at the end of the field season.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the field experiment.

claim: ICE 8 plants showed no growth difference to the empty vector control plants during the third field season.
source: ICE 8 plants showed no growth difference to the empty vector control plants.
evidence: This is stated in the context of the third field season sampling.

claim: The bacterial communities of all three compartments (bulk soil, root, and leaf) were clearly distinguishable by their species richness and diversities.
source: The bacterial communities of all three compartments were clearly distinguishable by their species richness and diversities (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Some of the leaf samples showed surprisingly low numbers of sequencing reads and overall very poor species richness.
source: Whereas root-associated communities showed the expected rarefaction patterns, some of the leaf samples showed surprisingly low numbers of sequencing reads and overall very poor species richness (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: The leaf samples were dominated by a single OTU (~90% relative abundance) and basically contained only the genus Bacillus (relative abundances between 97.9% and 99.1% for EV and the ICE line, respectively).
source: The leaf samples were dominated by a single OTU (~90% relative abundance) and basically contained only the genus Bacillus (relative abundances between 97.9% and 99.1% for EV and the ICE line, respectively).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the leaf sample composition.

claim: The dominant leaf OTU showed 100% sequence similarity to B. tequilensis and B. velezensis and 97.8% identity to B. pumilus DSM 1794.
source: This dominant leaf OTU showed 100% sequence similarity to B. tequilensis and B. velezensis and 97.8% identity to B. pumilus DSM 1794.
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence analysis.

claim: When high coverage leaf samples were included within the hierarchal clustering they indicated no separation by genotype.
source: Still, when we included the high coverage leaf samples within the hierarchal clustering they indicated no separation by genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the clustering analysis.

claim: The different compartments separated well across the first principal coordinate of the PCoA plot and indicated the highest sample variability and a potential influence by genotype within the root compartment.
source: The different compartments separated well across the first principal coordinate of the PCoA plot and indicated the highest sample variability and a potential influence by genotype within the root compartment (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The root-samples from the two genotypes showed highly similar diversities in the rarefaction analysis and a strong overlap of shared phylotypes.
source: The root-samples from the two genotypes showed again highly similar diversities in the rarefaction analysis and a strong overlap of shared phylotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: At the higher taxonomic levels, the root-associated microbiota of the ICE 8 and EV plants showed overall a similar composition of relative abundances with Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria as the dominating phyla.
source: At the higher taxonomic levels, the root-associated microbiota of the ICE 8 and EV plants showed overall a similar composition of relative abundances with Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria as the dominating phyla (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Sample grouping by the weighted and unweighted UniFrac distance, using principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) revealed no separation by genotype (p=0.19, ANOSIM).
source: Sample grouping by the weighted and unweighted UniFrac distance, using principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) revealed no separation by genotype (p=0.19, ANOSIM) (Figure 6C) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in figures.

claim: Within the Bacteriodetes the family of Sphingobacteriaceae showed a significant reduction in the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
source: Within the Bacteriodetes the family of Sphingobacteriaceae showed a significant reduction in the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
evidence: This is stated as a result of group significance comparisons.

claim: At the genus level, three different genera showed significant differences in their relative abundance between the genotypes.
source: At the genus level, three different genera showed significant differences in their relative abundance between the genotypes.
evidence: This is stated as a result of statistical analysis.

claim: 'Leifsonia' (Microbacteriaceae) and Pantoea (Enterobacteriaceae) showed an increase in relative abundance in the ICE line compared to the controls.
source: Interestingly, two of these showed an increase in relative abundance in the ICE line compared to the controls and were identified as 'Leifsonia' (Microbacteriaceae) and Pantoea (Enterobacteriaceae) (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The relatively large increase of Pantoea (6% relative abundance) could largely explain the dissimilar contributions of the family Enterobacteriaceae.
source: In particular, the relatively large increase of Pantoea (6% relative abundance) could largely explain the dissimilar contributions of the family Enterobacteriaceae.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The only genus which showed a reduction in relative abundance of about 1% within the transgenic lines was found within the Sphingobacteriaceae and matched to an uncultured clone within the 'Pedobacter_g3' group (96% sequence similarity to Pedobacter).
source: The only genus which showed a reduction in relative abundance of about 1% within the transgenic lines was found within the Sphingobacteriaceae and matched to an uncultured clone within the 'Pedobacter_g3' group (96% sequence similarity to Pedobacter).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: Bacillaceae showed very low relative abundances within the dataset and did not differ significantly between transgenic and control plants.
source: Bacillaceae however, showed very low relative abundances within the dataset and did not differ significantly between transgenic and control plants.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: The analyses of the alpha and beta diversities showed no genotype differences when separated by gram type (ANOSIM 'gram-positive' p=0.258, 'gram-negative' p=0.091).
source: The analyses of the alpha and beta diversities showed no genotype differences when separated by gram type (ANOSIM 'gram-positive' p=0.258, 'gram-negative' p=0.091) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated with statistical test results and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Consistent with the analysis of the entire dataset, 'Leifsonia', 'Pedobacter_g3' and Pantoea differed between the genotypes at the genus level.
source: Consistent with the analysis of the entire dataset, 'Leifsonia', 'Pedobacter_g3' and Pantoea differed between the genotypes at the genus level.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the split dataset analysis.

claim: Some low abundant groups (Dyadobacter, Erwinia and Chryseobacterium) showed differences as well within the 'gram-negative' taxa.
source: In addition, some low abundant groups (Dyadobacter, Erwinia and Chryseobacterium) showed differences as well within the 'gram-negative' taxa (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: When the same analysis was performed at the OTU level, only three OTUs (belonging to 'Leifsonia' and Patulibacter) differed significantly within the 'gram-positive' taxa.
source: When the same analysis was performed at the OTU level, only three OTUs (belonging to 'Leifsonia' and Patulibacter) differed significantly within the 'gram-positive' taxa.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the OTU-level analysis.

claim: None of the 'gram-negative' OTUs showed significant differences.
source: None of the 'gram-negative' OTUs showed significant differences (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B,C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The genus Bacillus was the only group within the 'gram-positive' taxa which showed at least a marginal tendency for reduction from 1.3% relative abundance in the controls to 0.2% relative abundance in the transgenic plants, though not statistically significant.
source: Interestingly, the genus Bacillus was the only group within the 'gram-positive' taxa which showed at least a marginal tendency for reduction from 1.3% relative abundance in the controls to 0.2% relative abundance in the transgenic plants, though not statistically significant (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,C).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Within the root samples, the genus Bacillus contained only a single OTU (OTU99) which showed 99.2% sequence identity to B. kribbensis and B. deserti and 97.4% identity to B. megaterium.
source: Within the root samples, the genus Bacillus contained only a single OTU (OTU99) which showed 99.2% sequence identity to B. kribbensis and B. deserti and 97.4% identity to B. megaterium.
evidence: This is stated as a result of sequence analysis.

claim: K. rhizophila showed no difference to the controls in infiltration assays.
source: But whereas K. rhizophila showed no difference to the controls, we observed for M. luteus at 2 dpi not a decrease but an unexpected increase in CFUs within the transgenic plants compared to the controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: M. luteus showed at 2 dpi not a decrease but an unexpected increase in CFUs within the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
source: But whereas K. rhizophila showed no difference to the controls, we observed for M. luteus at 2 dpi not a decrease but an unexpected increase in CFUs within the transgenic plants compared to the controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The M. luteus outcome was confirmed for both transgenic plant lines in an independent infiltration experiment.
source: This outcome was confirmed for both transgenic plant lines in an independent infiltration experiment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Two native Actinobacteria isolates (Arthrobacter sp. #S02 and Rhodococcus sp. #S05) showed no susceptibility to the peptide, even when isolated 6 days post inoculation.
source: Furthermore, we tested two native Actinobacteria isolates (Arthrobacter sp. #S02 and Rhodococcus sp. #S05) together with closely related strains from the German culture collection. Both genera are known for their ability to degrade and metabolize nicotine, the signature defensive secondary metabolite of the plant genus (Brandsch, 2006; Gong et al., 2009), but showed no susceptibility to the peptide, even when isolated 6 days post inoculation (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated with citations and shown in figures.

claim: None of the tested Actinobacteria showed a reduction in the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
source: Overall, none of the tested Actinobacteria showed a reduction in the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the Actinobacteria infiltration results.

claim: Most of the isolates belonged to the B. pumilus/B. safensis clade (strain #5, #45, #58 and #77) and showed very similar CFU reductions from 2 to 6 dpi, as the previously tested laboratory strain B. pumilus DSM 1794.
source: Most of the isolates belonged to the B. pumilus/B. safensis clade (strain #5, #45, #58 and #77) and showed very similar CFU reductions from 2 to 6 dpi, as the previously tested laboratory strain B. pumilus DSM 1794 (Figure 7A) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in figures.

claim: Only isolate #88 displayed overall weaker, but still significant reductions.
source: Only isolate #88 displayed overall weaker, but still significant reductions.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the infiltration assays.

claim: Consolidating all results from the B. pumilus/B. safensis clade, the antimicrobial activity of line ICE 8 tends to be stronger compared to line ICE 6.
source: Consolidating all results from this clade, the antimicrobial activity of line ICE 8 tends to be stronger compared to line ICE 6 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Experimental infiltrations with B. megaterium type strain DSM 32 indicated no significant CFU reduction effects.
source: Experimental infiltrations with another Bacillus group (B. megaterium) indicated for the type strain DSM 32 no significant CFU reduction effects, whereas the B. megaterium isolate #38 revealed high levels of susceptibility (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The B. megaterium isolate #38 revealed high levels of susceptibility.
source: Experimental infiltrations with another Bacillus group (B. megaterium) indicated for the type strain DSM 32 no significant CFU reduction effects, whereas the B. megaterium isolate #38 revealed high levels of susceptibility (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: B. megaterium isolate #7 and #38 showed strong susceptibilities, but isolate #126 and #131 showed no significant reductions.
source: This revealed strong susceptibilities for isolate #7 and #38, but no significant reductions for isolate #126 and #131 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The distinct levels of susceptibility among B. megaterium isolates were particularly remarkable, since these isolates were nearly indistinguishable by their 16S rDNA sequences.
source: These distinct levels of susceptibility were particularly remarkable, since these isolates were nearly indistinguishable by their 16S rDNA sequences (Figure 7A, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated and supported by sequence data.

claim: The obtained CFU counts of both B. megaterium strains (#38 and #7) showed no significant differences between the transgenic and control plants in long-term colonization experiments.
source: To test if such susceptibilities would persist in a long-term colonization experiment as root-endophytes, we inoculated seeds with the two most susceptible B. megaterium strains (#38 and #7) and re-isolated the bacteria from surface sterilized roots after 4 weeks of growth. The obtained CFU counts of both strains showed no significant differences between the transgenic and control plants (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: Both 'root re-isolated' and 'naïve' strains showed the same susceptibility and showed no indication for the development of peptide resistance within the transgenic plants.
source: As we hypothesized that the bacteria could have developed AMP resistance within the roots due to the longer exposure to the peptide, we compared the 'root re-isolated' strain against the 'naïve' strain in a leaf infiltration assay. Both strains showed the same susceptibility and showed no indication for the development of peptide resistance within the transgenic plants (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The root-associated microbial communities of field-grown N. attenuata plants were mainly dominated by the phyla Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria, which together account for 80% of the obtained sequences.
source: The root-associated microbial communities of field-grown N. attenuata plants were mainly dominated by the phyla Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria, which together account for 80% of the obtained sequences (Figure 6B), a commonly observed pattern from the root communities of other plant species (Bulgarelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Previous studies in Arabidopsis and maize have shown that the composition of the endophytic microbial community of these plants is mainly influenced by soil type and geographic location, whereas the plant genotype or ecotype had only a minor influence.
source: Previous studies in Arabidopsis and maize have shown that the composition of the endophytic microbial community of these plants is mainly influenced by soil type and geographic location, whereas the plant genotype or ecotype had only a minor influence (Bulgarelli et al., 2012; Lundberg et al., 2012; Peiffer et al., 2013; Schlaeppi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Comparing isogenic plants in the field, we observed no major differences within their root-associated communities.
source: In contrast, we analyzed isogenic plants, which differed only in a single trait. Comparing these plants in the field, we observed no major differences within their root-associated communities.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the field experiment.

claim: Firmicutes showed a rather low relative abundance (0.6%) in the dataset.
source: Unfortunately, Firmicutes which were the main target group for the generation of AMP expressing plants showed a rather low relative abundance (0.6%) in our dataset (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Bacilli were believed to be important mutualists of N. attenuata, as they dominated the culturable community with up to 63% relative abundance in a previous study.
source: Bacilli were believed to be important mutualists of N. attenuata, as they dominated the culturable community with up to 63% relative abundance in a previous study (Long et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: Most recent NGS sequencing datasets are now pointing to much lower estimates and Firmicutes are therefore no longer considered as a major root inhabiting group.
source: Still, most recent NGS sequencing datasets are now pointing to much lower estimates and Firmicutes are therefore no longer considered as a major root inhabiting group (Müller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The studies of Wagner et al. (2016) and Robertson-Albertyn et al. (2017) showed <1% relative abundance for Firmicutes in root and rhizosphere samples, when using the Illumina sequencing platform together with the primers 515F/806R.
source: The studies of Wagner et al. (2016) and Robertson-Albertyn et al. (2017) showed <1% relative abundance for Firmicutes in root and rhizosphere samples, when using the Illumina sequencing platform together with the primers 515F/806R.
evidence: This is stated with citations to specific studies.

claim: Other studies even reported a potential exclusion of Firmicutes from the roots of Arabidopsis and barley, as the levels in the endosphere compartment (<1% abundance) were lower than that of the surrounding soil.
source: Other studies even reported a potential exclusion of Firmicutes from the roots of Arabidopsis and barley, as the levels in the endosphere compartment (<1% abundance) were lower than that of the surrounding soil (Bulgarelli et al., 2012, Bulgarelli et al., 2015; Bodenhausen et al., 2013; Schlaeppi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations.

claim: In a previous study, we analyzed the microbial communities of wild N. attenuata populations and observed a similar trend, where Firmicutes represented about 4.5% of the community in the bulk soil but only 0.5% for the root compartments of N. attenuata.
source: In a previous study, we analyzed the microbial communities of wild N. attenuata populations and observed a similar trend, where Firmicutes represented about 4.5% of the community in the bulk soil but only 0.5% for the root compartments of N. attenuata (Santhanam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: A few studies had investigated if transgenic plants expressing antimicrobial agents would influence plant-beneficial microbial communities, but never found clear genotype-effects.
source: A few studies had investigated if transgenic plants expressing antimicrobial agents would influence plant-beneficial microbial communities, but never found clear genotype-effects (Meyer et al., 2013; Turner et al., 2013; Kaur et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to previous studies.

claim: The feasibility of microbiome manipulation within native ecosystems appears to be more challenging than previously assumed.
source: The feasibility of microbiome manipulation within native ecosystems appears to be more challenging than previously assumed, and even the massive application of antibiotics, as commonly done in apple orchards, had surprisingly little effect on the composition of the microbial community in soil (Shade et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a study on antibiotic application.

claim: Even the massive application of antibiotics, as commonly done in apple orchards, had surprisingly little effect on the composition of the microbial community in soil.
source: The feasibility of microbiome manipulation within native ecosystems appears to be more challenging than previously assumed, and even the massive application of antibiotics, as commonly done in apple orchards, had surprisingly little effect on the composition of the microbial community in soil (Shade et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Even the direct treatment of apple flowers with streptomycin, resulted in no observable change in the microbiome compositions.
source: Even the direct treatment of apple flowers with streptomycin, resulted in no observable change in the microbiome compositions (Shade et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The ectopic expression of this AMP in a solanaceous species has the advantage of obviating previous adaptations of native microbial communities.
source: Ectopic expression of this AMP in a solanaceous species has the advantage of obviating previous adaptations of native microbial communities.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental approach.

claim: AMPs have rarely been reported to be natively expressed in roots.
source: Moreover, the ectopic expression also provided another dimension: AMPs have rarely been reported to be natively expressed in roots.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: In plants, the majority of AMPs have been isolated from seeds, followed by flowers, fruits, stems or leaves.
source: In plants, the majority of AMPs have been isolated from seeds, followed by flowers, fruits, stems or leaves (Carvalho and Gomes, 2009; Nawrot et al., 2014; Molesini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: The heterologously expressed peptide showed a lower accumulation in roots compared to leaves.
source: Although we were able to clearly detect the heterologously expressed peptide within the root system, it showed a lower accumulation in this compartment compared to leaves.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: The lower peptide accumulation in roots may explain why root effects were not apparent in the transgenic plants while leaf antimicrobial effects could be readily determined.
source: This may explain why root effects were not apparent in the transgenic plants while leaf antimicrobial effects could be readily determined.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the observation.

claim: After three field seasons, the ectopic expression of the antimicrobial peptide Mc-AMP1 does not influence plant growth, flower production or herbivore infestation of transgenic N. attenuata plants, or has any other observable negative effects on the plants when grown in the native environment.
source: After three field seasons, we can conclude that the ectopic expression of the antimicrobial peptide Mc-AMP1 does not influence plant growth, flower production or herbivore infestation of transgenic N. attenuata plants, or has any other observable negative effects on the plants when grown in the native environment.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from multiple field seasons.

claim: Although antibacterial effects could be demonstrated in the glasshouse in leaves, they were not apparent for roots and these experiments highlight that the in planta manipulation of complex microbial communities is a much more challenging endeavor than commonly believed.
source: Although antibacterial effects could be demonstrated in the glasshouse in leaves, they were not apparent for roots and these experiments highlight that the in planta manipulation of complex microbial communities is a much more challenging endeavor than commonly believed.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Knottins are reported to exhibit activity against gram-positive, but not gram-negative bacteria.
source: Knottins are reported to exhibit activity against gram-positive, but not gram-negative bacteria (Pelegrini et al., 2011), which would make them a promising candidate for the manipulation of the host-microbe relationship.
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Activity of antibiotics against laboratory strains does not commonly reflect a similar effectiveness against native bacteria.
source: Activity of antibiotics against laboratory strains does not commonly reflect a similar effectiveness against native bacteria (Wright, 2007) and for different ecosystems, the diverse communities of soil bacteria have shown to harbor non-anthropogenic resistance to various antibiotics (Cytryn, 2013; Shade et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: For different ecosystems, the diverse communities of soil bacteria have shown to harbor non-anthropogenic resistance to various antibiotics.
source: Activity of antibiotics against laboratory strains does not commonly reflect a similar effectiveness against native bacteria (Wright, 2007) and for different ecosystems, the diverse communities of soil bacteria have shown to harbor non-anthropogenic resistance to various antibiotics (Cytryn, 2013; Shade et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: AMP expressing grapevine plants showed promising resistance against a single pathogen strain in the glasshouse, but failed to display these effects in the field.
source: As demonstrated in a previous study, AMP expressing grapevine plants showed promising resistance against a single pathogen strain in the glasshouse, but failed to display these effects in the field, which is consistent with an underestimated resilience of native pathovars (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: The plant apoplast is an environment that is very different from that of petri dishes.
source: The plant apoplast is an environment that is very different from that of petri dishes, and even though activity tests ex vivo had been traditionally used to confirm correct peptide folding, they are less informative than the evaluation of whether growth inhibition could be expected within the plant.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: Despite the strong peptide accumulations within the leaves, only about half of the tested bacterial strains showed a reduction in the experimental infiltrations.
source: We could demonstrate activity against several Bacillus strains under physiological conditions of the leaf apoplast. But despite the strong peptide accumulations within the leaves, only about half of the tested bacterial strains showed a reduction in the experimental infiltrations (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Micrococcus luteus showed the opposite effect with an increase in CFU numbers within the transgenic plants.
source: Noteworthy is Micrococcus luteus, which is supposed to be susceptible to this AMP from in vitro reports, but showed the opposite effect with an increase in CFU numbers within the transgenic plants.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: AMP activity can change or vanish in planta due to salt concentrations, protease-based degradation or the inhibition by phenolic compounds.
source: It has frequently been shown that AMP activity changes or vanishes in planta due to salt concentrations, protease-based degradation or the inhibition by phenolic compounds (Zeitler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: AMPs are notoriously sensitive to divalent cations and their activity can be drastically reduced due to small amounts of Ca2 or Mg2 within the apoplast.
source: AMPs are notoriously sensitive to divalent cations and their activity can be drastically reduced due to small amounts of Ca2 or Mg2 within the apoplast (De Bolle et al., 1996; Güell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Micrococcus is usually known for its exquisite sensitivity to many antibiotics (i.e. lysozyme and insect defensins) and is commonly used as indicator strain for antimicrobial activity.
source: As Micrococcus is usually known for its exquisite sensitivity to many antibiotics (i.e. lysozyme and insect defensins) it is commonly used as indicator strain for antimicrobial activity (Fleming and Allison, 1922; Cociancich et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Most of the Bacillus isolates showed clear reduction effects within the leaf infiltration assay.
source: In contrast, we observed for most of the Bacillus isolates clear reduction effects within the leaf infiltration assay, which enabled us to use this method as a high throughput screening to select for transgenic plants with antimicrobial activity.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the experiments.

claim: There was a surprising heterogeneity of resistance among closely related Bacillus isolates.
source: This confirmed not only that the plants have in planta activity against Firmicutes but showed also a surprising heterogeneity of resistance among closely related isolates.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the infiltration experiments.

claim: The B. megaterium isolates were practically indistinguishable when compared by their near entire 16S rDNA sequence.
source: This was rather remarkable as these strains showed a high phylogenetic relatedness and were practically indistinguishable when compared by their near entire 16S rDNA sequence (Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated and supported by sequence data.

claim: Antimicrobial peptides are reported to target multiple essential structures of the bacterial cell, and the development of resistance mechanisms is usually considered unlikely.
source: Since antimicrobial peptides are reported to target multiple essential structures of the bacterial cell, the development of resistance mechanisms is usually considered unlikely, but differences in slime capsule formation or surface charge modifications are possible explanations for the observed discrepancies among these isolates (Nawrocki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Differences in slime capsule formation or surface charge modifications are possible explanations for the observed discrepancies among isolates.
source: Since antimicrobial peptides are reported to target multiple essential structures of the bacterial cell, the development of resistance mechanisms is usually considered unlikely, but differences in slime capsule formation or surface charge modifications are possible explanations for the observed discrepancies among these isolates (Nawrocki et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation as a possible explanation.

claim: The grouping into OTUs is a technical necessarily, but it can mask a surprising diversity of ecological heterogeneity and rarely resembles a true monophyletic group.
source: The grouping into OTUs is a technical necessarily, but it can mask a surprising diversity of ecological heterogeneity and rarely resembles a true monophyletic group (Koeppel and Wu, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The use of single isolates allows to determine individual isolate functions within a population.
source: Whereas the use of single isolates is a rather simple means of accessing this diversity, it can be very rewarding as it allows to determine individual isolate functions within a population (Savory et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: An exposure to a low AMP concentration for 4 weeks has been shown to be sufficient to select for strains with higher AMP resistance in other studies.
source: An exposure to a low AMP concentration for 4 weeks has been shown to be sufficient to select for strains with higher AMP resistance in other studies (Dobson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: We found no evidence consistent with the hypothesis that bacteria might develop resistances when they reside as a root endophyte within an AMP expressing plant.
source: However, the 'root re-isolated' strain did not differ in susceptibility compared to the original 'naïve' strain, as compared in a leaf infiltration assay, and we found no evidence consistent with the hypothesis that bacteria might develop resistances when they reside as a root endophyte within an AMP expressing plant (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments and shown in the figure supplement.

claim: The results of single strain inoculations are likely poor predictors of the potential effects of AMP expression on the composition of the native community within the field.
source: Clearly the results of single strain inoculations are likely poor predictors of the potential effects of AMP expression on the composition of the native community within the field.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: Firmicutes have been described for years as an important and large group of plant endophytes based on culturable approaches.
source: Bacilli have been described for years as an important and large group of plant endophytes based on culturable approaches (Hardoim et al., 2015; Levy et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations.

claim: Most recent NGS sequencing datasets are now pointing to much lower estimates and Firmicutes are therefore no longer considered as a major root inhabiting group.
source: Still, most recent NGS sequencing datasets are now pointing to much lower estimates and Firmicutes are therefore no longer considered as a major root inhabiting group (Müller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Firmicutes represented about 4.5% of the community in the bulk soil but only 0.5% for the root compartments of N. attenuata in a previous study.
source: In a previous study, we analyzed the microbial communities of wild N. attenuata populations and observed a similar trend, where Firmicutes represented about 4.5% of the community in the bulk soil but only 0.5% for the root compartments of N. attenuata (Santhanam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous study.

claim: The genus 'Pedobacter_g3' within the Sphingobacteriaceae was the only group which showed within the ICE lines, a significant reduction in relative abundance compared to the controls.
source: The genus 'Pedobacter_g3' within the Sphingobacteriaceae was the only group which showed within the ICE lines, a significant reduction in relative abundance compared to the controls.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: The presence of sphingolipids could be a potential susceptibility factor and a binding site for antimicrobial peptides.
source: The presence of sphingolipids (the eponymous characteristic of this group) could be a potential susceptibility factor and a binding site for antimicrobial peptides (Thevissen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citation as a possible explanation.

claim: Sequence read numbers matching the genera 'Leifsonia' (Microbacteriaceae) and Pantoea (Enterobacteriaceae) were significantly increased within the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
source: Interestingly, sequence read numbers matching the genera 'Leifsonia' (Microbacteriaceae) and Pantoea (Enterobacteriaceae) were significantly increased within the transgenic plants compared to the controls.
evidence: This is stated as a result of the analysis.

claim: The genus Pantoea showed a particularly large increase in relative abundance of 6%.
source: The genus Pantoea showed a particularly large increase in relative abundance of 6%.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative result.

claim: Both genera Leifsonia and Pantoea are known to contain plant pathogenic as well as beneficial bacteria.
source: Whereas the reduction of mutualists would account for an increase in pathogens, both genera are known to contain plant pathogenic as well as beneficial bacteria and the resolution of the sequencing data does not allow inferences regarding function.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The acquisition of virulence plasmids can be sufficient for the transition from plant beneficial to phytopathogenic status.
source: As recently shown, the acquisition of virulence plasmids can be sufficient for the transition from plant beneficial to phytopathogenic status (Savory et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The exclusion of a single keystone species can be sufficient to influence the composition of the entire community.
source: Greenhouse experiments with artificial communities showed that the exclusion of a single keystone species can be sufficient to influence the composition of the entire community (Niu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Under certain growth conditions AMP expression could result in an unintended increase of potential pathogenic bacteria.
source: Little attention has been paid to microbe-microbe interactions and the importance of antagonistic mutualisms or antibiosis effects, and it cannot be excluded that under certain growth conditions AMP expression could result in an unintended increase of potential pathogenic bacteria.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about possible consequences.

claim: The majority of commensals in the human gut flora proved to be remarkably resilient to inflammation-associated AMPs.
source: This reminds us of the findings within the human gut flora, where the majority of commensals proved to be remarkably resilient to inflammation-associated AMPs (Cullen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: The tremendous diversity of environmental bacteria, and their rich reservoir of genetic variability, allows natural communities to withstand antimicrobial activity and act as a single cohesive unit of antibiotic resistance.
source: The tremendous diversity of environmental bacteria, and their rich reservoir of genetic variability, allows natural communities to withstand antimicrobial activity and act as a single cohesive unit of antibiotic resistance as shown for marine environments (Cordero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Small mobile elements (e.g. vectors with resistance genes) can easily spread within a native microbial community, resulting in dramatic changes of resistance, with few observable shifts in the distribution of taxa.
source: Small mobile elements (e.g. vectors with resistance genes) can easily spread within a native microbial community, resulting in dramatic changes of resistance, with few observable shifts in the distribution of taxa.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge.

claim: The Illumina sequencing platform has (together with the 515F/806R primer pair) become a widely used and universally accepted system for high throughput 16S rDNA profiling of bacterial communities.
source: Currently, the Illumina sequencing platform has (together with the 515F/806R primer pair) become a widely used and universally accepted system for high throughput 16S rDNA profiling of bacterial communities; however, these relative short amplicons limit the phylogenetic resolution and thwarts the characterization of intraspecific variations (van der Heijden and Schlaeppi, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Short amplicons limit the phylogenetic resolution and thwarts the characterization of intraspecific variations.
source: Currently, the Illumina sequencing platform has (together with the 515F/806R primer pair) become a widely used and universally accepted system for high throughput 16S rDNA profiling of bacterial communities; however, these relative short amplicons limit the phylogenetic resolution and thwarts the characterization of intraspecific variations (van der Heijden and Schlaeppi, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: N. attenuata seeds showed no vertically transmitted microbes, and hence are considered to be born sterile.
source: N. attenuata seeds showed no vertically transmitted microbes, and hence are considered to be born sterile (Santhanam et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation.

claim: Roots are colonize by bacteria within a few days of planting, and can acquire full microbiomes within about two weeks.
source: As reported previously for rice, roots are colonize by bacteria within a few days of planting, and can acquire full microbiomes within about two weeks (Edwards et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a study on rice.
